articles.title: Stonehenge Altar Stone remains a mystery as theory overturned
articles.summary: It was thought the Stonehenge artefact was from north east Scotland but a new study disputes that.
articles.body:
A new study exploring the origins of the six tonne Altar Stone at Stonehenge has ruled out a theory that it came from an area of Scotland.

The 4.9 metre sandstone slab within the circle was initially believed to have originated in Wales until a more recent study pointed towards it coming from north east Scotland.

Scientific tests were carried out in the Orcadian Basin area of Scotland, but researchers failed to find a location with the same characteristics of the stone in that area.

However study lead, Professor Duncan Pirrie from the University of South Wales, said the latest investigation has left them "far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer."

'Greatest' military air show leaves RAF Fairford

Expelled councillor vows 'I will always be Labour'

New mental health centre could open in town

Pirrie said his latest publication on the Altar Stone has "built the clearest picture yet" and was "the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken".

Professor Nick Pearce from Aberystwyth University, who worked on the previous research, said "ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones".

The geochemistry expert said: "Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated.

"The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago."

The world-famous Wiltshire monument was constructed in multiple phases between 3000 and 1600BC. However, not all stones come from the area.

The smaller bluestones travelled around 225km from west Wales with research suggesting a few were taken directly from another circle.

The latest study combined new observations and looked at fragments of the stone in museum collections, examining structure, minerals and composition.

It has been published in the Journal of the Geological Society.

articles.title: Did Russia rehearse satellite attack? Expert on close encounter with western spacecraft
articles.summary: A Russian military satellite that moved dangerously close to a western commercial spacecraft last month may have been testing capabilities for a potential
articles.body: A Russian military satellite that moved dangerously close to a western commercial spacecraft last month may have been testing capabilities for a potential attack, a military space expert has warned. Meanwhile, two other Russian satellites linked to the spacecraft are reportedly moving towards the orbital path of another western satellite, according to the Reuters.US under secretary of State Thomas DiNanno said in a post on X following the incident in mid-October that Russia's cosmos 2612 military satellite had been "intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite". He described the activity as being "consistent with on-orbit weapons operations".According to the news agency Reuters, the satellite targeted during the encounter, known as X36, is operated by Finnish company ICEYE. It supplies radar imagery to western governments and military organisations, including Ukraine.Three space experts described the encounter as one of the closest known approaches by a Russian military spacecraft to a commercial satellite operating in low Earth orbit.Greg Gillinger, a senior space analyst at US-based Integrity ISR, which provides training to American space forces, said the manoeuvre appeared to resemble preparations for an attack."This is the most aggressive posture I've seen Russia take in terms of threatening satellites from another nation," he told Reuters.Russia's defence ministry did not respond to a request for comment. Moscow has repeatedly warned that commercial Western satellites providing assistance to Ukraine could be considered legitimate targets for retaliatory action.Ann Stevens, head of ICEYE's US operations, told Reuters that X36 "has been and will continue to be a productive satellite". She added that the company's network of radar-imaging satellites was designed to remain resilient in the event of disruptions.Growing concerns over weapons in spaceThe incident has intensified concerns about the security of commercial satellite networks, which have become increasingly important to military operations.It follows months of Russian activity around ICEYE satellites. Western officials have warned that such manoeuvres demonstrate capabilities that could potentially be used to threaten or disrupt commercial satellite networks, including those operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX.Gillinger, a former US air force intelligence officer who has been monitoring Russian spacecraft, believes Cosmos 2612 may have been testing capabilities associated with kinetic attacks. He argued that such an extremely close approach would not have been necessary for routine intelligence gathering or electronic interference.According to US space intelligence company slingshot aerospace, Cosmos 2612 is publicly classified as a satellite designed for servicing and inspecting other spacecraft.It is among six military satellites Russia launched in April. Space analysts have said that four of these spacecraft moved close to ICEYE's X36 satellite in May.ICEYE subsequently repositioned X36, prompting additional manoeuvres by Russian satellites, the company's chief executive, Rafal Modrzewski, told Reuters in September.In early October, Cosmos 2612 positioned itself several hundred kilometres behind X36, according to space analysts. Over the following days, it rapidly reduced the distance, approaching within approximately one kilometre (half a mile) of the commercial spacecraft around the middle of the month. Some analysts estimated that the separation was only a few hundred metres or even less.Gillinger said Cosmos 2612 later moved approximately 400 kilometres (250 miles) away from X36.He added that two other Russian satellites belonging to the same group were now moving towards the orbital path of another ICEYE spacecraft, identified as X37.US-based space-tracking company COMSPOC also reported that the two Russian satellites were increasingly well positioned to approach X37. Public space-object catalogues identify both X36 and X37 as spacecraft registered in the United States.Experts warn of potential disruption to satellitesGermany's space commander, Major General Michael Traut, told Reuters that close encounters such as the one involving Cosmos 2612 could serve several purposes, including inspecting, observing or interfering with another spacecraft, depending on its technological capabilities."We must therefore consider the entire spectrum of possible effects, ranging from temporarily disrupting a satellite's operations to permanently disabling it," he said.However, Traut cautioned that the ability to carry out such orbital manoeuvres did not automatically indicate that Russia was preparing for or rehearsing an attack.He added that publicly available orbital information alone was insufficient to establish the actual purpose behind the satellite's movements.Major powers prepare for possible space conflictThe latest developments come amid growing concerns that geopolitical tensions could increasingly extend beyond Earth.Major powers are preparing for the possibility of military confrontations in space. Washington recently acknowledged deploying weapons in orbit, while the head of US Space Command said earlier this year that Russia had placed a space weapon within striking distance of critical American national security satellites.Andrew Turner, a space consultant and retired senior British air force officer, said Russia's manoeuvre near X36 had significantly increased the possibility of an attack, whether through deliberate action or an unintended interaction between spacecraft.The incident has highlighted the growing risks facing commercial satellites that support military operations and the challenges of protecting critical space infrastructure as countries expand their capabilities in orbit.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2023, American singer-songwriter Jimmy Buffett left an estimated $275 million trust for his family; three years later, his widow and longtime adviser are fighting over its control
articles.summary: When music legend Jimmy Buffett died in September 2023, he left behind more than a catalogue of hit songs and a business empire built around the
articles.body: When music legend Jimmy Buffett died in September 2023, he left behind more than a catalogue of hit songs and a business empire built around the Margaritaville brand. As reported by PEOPLE, his reported $275 million trust was intended to provide for his wife of 46 years, Jane Slagsvol, and their three children. But nearly three years after his death, the arrangements he made have become the subject of a bitter legal dispute. Jane is seeking to remove longtime financial adviser Richard Mozenter as co-trustee, while Buffett's children have taken differing positions on who should manage their father's fortune.Legal battle over managing Jimmy Buffett's wealth after his deathBuffett, best known for songs such as Margaritaville, built a career that extended well beyond music. His business interests included restaurants, hotels, merchandise and other ventures associated with the Margaritaville brand. By the time of his death at 76 in September 2023, his financial interests had grown into a substantial estate.Before his death, Buffett appointed his wife of 46 years, Jane Slagsvol, and longtime adviser Richard Mozenter to serve as co-trustees of his trust. Their responsibilities included overseeing its assets and ensuring that distributions were handled according to the arrangements he had established.Why Savannah Buffett wants her father's wishes honoured in estate battleSavannah Buffett, the eldest of the singer's three children, has taken a position that differs from her mother's. She opposes Jane's attempt to remove Mozenter and wants him to remain involved in managing the trust.Reportedly, at a February 12, 2026, hearing in Palm Beach, Savannah's lawyer, Jared Gelles, told the court that his client wanted her father's original decision to be respected. He argued that Mozenter was not someone brought into the family’s financial affairs shortly before Buffett's death, but an adviser with years of experience and a detailed understanding of the singer's business and personal arrangements.Gelles described Mozenter as one of the people who had been deeply involved in Buffett's world for a long time. His argument centred on the value of that institutional knowledge, particularly when dealing with a complicated collection of assets.Savannah Buffett's $75 million inheritance disputeSavannah's disagreement with her mother has also been linked to an earlier controversy involving the possibility of disinheritance.The issue surfaced in legal filings in August 2025, when lawyers representing Mozenter submitted screenshots of alleged text exchanges between Jane and Savannah. The messages appeared to suggest that Jane had threatened to remove her eldest daughter from the trust.In one exchange presented to the court, Jane allegedly referred to the $75 million that Savannah could potentially lose, suggesting that her financial interest should be a reason for her to behave more like her siblings. Another message reportedly included the words, "Say good bye to that 75mil".During an August 18, 2025, hearing, Jane's legal representatives rejected the suggestion that she had taken steps to disinherit her children. They also said she had no intention of doing so, while acknowledging that the trust's terms gave her the legal authority to make such a decision.Cameron and Delaney focus on protecting the trust's assetsBuffett's other two children, Cameron and Delaney, have approached the dispute from a different angle. Rather than openly supporting either Jane or Mozenter in the disagreement over the co-trustee position, they have concentrated on the financial condition of the trust and its ability to meet obligations over time.The siblings have retained separate legal representation from Savannah. Their lawyer, Peter Sachs, told the court in February that his clients wanted to ensure their mother received the financial support their father had intended. At the same time, they were concerned about preserving enough of the trust's value for the other beneficiaries.Sachs also raised a point about the nature of the estate. Although its reported value is around $275 million, he explained that the trust should not be treated as if the entire amount were readily available in cash.Their lawyer made clear that they were not taking sides in the personal and legal conflict between the two co-trustees. Their position is centred on the long-term administration of the estate rather than backing one individual over the other.Legal proceedings continue over control of Buffett's legacyThe dispute has continued through several court proceedings since 2025. In a more recent development, Jane appealed an order connected to the February 12 hearing that allows Mozenter to use trust funds for reasonable legal fees and related expenses arising from the litigation.The decision is significant because it concerns the use of the very assets both sides are seeking to protect. As the legal disagreement continues, the costs of resolving it also become part of the financial questions surrounding the estate.For now, his three children have not presented a united position on how the trust should be administered. Savannah wants Mozenter to retain his role, while Cameron and Delaney are concentrating on financial stability without endorsing either side. All three, however, have expressed a desire to see their mother receive the support their father intended.Disclaimer: This article is based on information publicly available. articles.title: Ranbir Kapoor in Ramayana: India's costliest film retells a beloved Hindu epic - but divides critics
articles.summary: Easily the most anticipated Bollywood film of the year, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the first of two parts.
articles.body:
India's most expensive film - a lavish retelling of the Hindu epic Ramayana, made in two parts for a reported $500m (£370m) - has opened in cinemas worldwide, sparking enormous expectations and mixed reviews.

Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the first of two planned films, a sprawling production that brings together some of India's biggest stars, Hollywood visual-effects expertise and two Oscar-winning composers in an attempt to take one of the country's most revered stories to a global audience.

One of Hinduism's foundational epics, the Ramayana has travelled across centuries and continents, finding expression in poetry, temple sculpture, shadow puppetry, folk theatre and stories passed down through generations. It has outlasted kingdoms and empires, inspired religious devotion and political movements, and found new life, again and again, on TV and in cinema.

Tiwari's version returns to the familiar story of love, duty, exile and war, set in a world of gods and demons, celestial weapons and mighty kingdoms.

Ranbir Kapoor plays Lord Ram, the virtuous prince of Ayodhya. Banished from his kingdom for 14 years, he retreats to the forest with his wife Sita (played by Sai Pallavi), who is kidnapped by Ravana, the 10-headed king of Lanka.

Played by Yash, one of southern India's biggest stars, Ravana is a powerful warrior whose pride leads him into an epic battle with Ram (which will be depicted in part 2, set to release next year).

The film's producer, Namit Malhotra, heads visual-effects company DNEG , which has worked on Hollywood blockbusters including Dune and Interstellar. The music is a collaboration between AR Rahman, the Oscar-winning Indian composer of Slumdog Millionaire, and Hans Zimmer, whose scores for Gladiator, The Dark Knight and Dune have helped define the sound of modern Hollywood.

The film opened days ahead of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights which celebrates Ram's return to Ayodhya after his exile.

But the critical response so far has been mixed.

Saibal Chatterjee of NDTV channel gave it three out of five stars, saying its visual spectacle often overshadowed the story. Its enormous scale, he wrote, "remains, for the most part, the only thing that stands out", while the acting remains "wildly inconsistent".

Rishabh Suri of the Hindustan Times newspaper was more enthusiastic, awarding it four stars.

"I am happy to report, all that money shows on screen," he wrote, praising the performances and visual effects, though he found the first half sluggish and the music underwhelming.

Shubhra Gupta of The Indian Express, who gave the film three stars, confessed to initial misgivings about its extravagant scale but found herself gradually won over, calling it the "perfect epic".

There was "enough sorcery and thrills and adventure" to sustain the spectacle, she wrote, and the filmmakers had managed to tell a sprawling story without being swallowed by it.

Internationally, too, the film drew contrasting reactions.

Writing in The Guardian, Peter Bradshaw called it a "thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama". He found echoes of Shakespeare in the royal intrigue that sends Rama into exile, and of Homer in his quest to rescue Sita. Its sweeping landscapes and fantastical imagery reminded him of The Lord of the Rings and The Lion King.

"It's a rather amazing adventure," he wrote , giving it four stars.

Others were less impressed. Siddhant Adlakha of IGN scored the film four out of 10, describing its action as "clunky" and its computer-generated imagery as an "eye-sore".

Giovanni Lago of Next Best Picture, who gave it five out of 10, praised Yash's magnetic Ravana and the score by Rahman and Zimmer. But he felt the film's vast narrative might have been better served by a Game of Thrones-style series.

The use of AI to adjust actors' lip movements for the English-language version also drew criticism. While Tiwari said it was intended to make the film more accessible to international audiences, Adlakha likened the result to "exaggerated mouth movements superimposed on still images for comedy sketches".

In India, the film has invited comparisons with earlier adaptations, particularly Ramanand Sagar's Ramayan, which captivated the country nearly four decades ago with simple sets and special effects that now seem quaint.

When the series first aired in 1987, Sunday mornings across India took on an almost devotional stillness.

Streets emptied, shops lowered their shutters and neighbours crowded around TV sets. Some viewers bathed, lit incense and garlanded their screens before the broadcast, preparing for the show much as they might for worship.

Arvind Rajagopal, a media scholar at New York University, told the BBC in 2019 that trains and buses would stop and passengers disembark to watch the show on roadside TVs.

Broadcast on the state-run Doordarshan network, some of the most popular parts of the 78-episode series drew an estimated 80-100 million viewers, astonishing numbers at a time when owning a TV was a luxury in India.

The actors, too, became objects of reverence. Arun Govil, who played Ram, has recalled people weeping at the sight of him and touching his feet. Now, in a casting choice brimming with nostalgia, Govil returns in Tiwari's film as Dasharatha, Ram's father.

Other adaptations found their own ways to reimagine the epic. The 1992 Indo-Japanese animated film Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama brought the tale to life through richly detailed, hand-drawn animation.

Tiwari's Ramayana arrives with technological resources its predecessors could barely have imagined - but also with the expectations of generations who have grown up with the story and its characters.

It also comes at a politically charged moment in India, where Ram has become a powerful symbol of Hindu identity - over the past decade and a half, even popular analyses or retellings of the epic have landed in controversy.

The 2023 film Adipurush , another big-budget retelling of Ramayana, sparked backlash on several fronts.

Hindu groups called for a ban, accusing it of disrespecting religious figures, while some critics questioned its depiction of Ravana, which they said drew on Mughal imagery and reinforced stereotypes about Muslims. The film was also criticised for its dialogue and visual effects.

For the actors portraying these characters in the latest film, that burden was deeply felt.

"I was filled with fear," Kapoor told the BBC Asian Network's Haroon Rashid. "I knew that maybe I'm too old for this. I won't be able to do justice to it."

He called the role "an opportunity of a lifetime", but said playing a figure worshipped by millions left little room for the creative freedom he had enjoyed in other films.

Sai Pallavi, who plays Sita, said the experience was as much spiritual as artistic. Raised in a religious household, she said she approached the part not just as a performance, but as an opportunity for personal growth.

How the film is being received will become clearer soon, as audiences head to cinemas.

But whatever the verdict, it marks a major cultural moment for India, bringing a story loved for generations to the big screen on an unprecedented scale.

articles.title: Second buyer makes rescue bid for Poundland as retailer faces collapse
articles.summary: A little-known investment group has made a bid to buy the business.
articles.body:
A second buyer has made a rescue bid for Poundland as the discount retailer teeters on the brink of collapse, with thousands of jobs at risk.

London-based Xyra Group has offered to pay off half of Poundland's outstanding debts - a key sticking point in takeover talks so far - immediately. The rest would be deferred.

With Poundland close to collapse, US-based owners Gordon Brothers have already rejected a rival bid from an Irish property group which would have saved its 12,000 staff.

Gordon Brothers said the business has faced years of instability and "remains challenged and vulnerable".

Sources familiar with the offer said Xyra is offering to immediately pay off £12.5m of an outstanding £30m loan on Poundland's books.

The offer came as Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds held crunch talks with Gordon Brothers about the future of the business, urging the investment firm to protect staff however possible.

Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for £1 last June, committed at the meeting to prioritise offers which protect its shops and workers.

The company said: "We are pursuing all avenues through the sale process to find a solution which protects as many jobs as possible and preserves value. Work continues at pace, engaging in active discussions on offers with interested parties."

Xyra is offering to pay off a higher proportion of Poundland's outstanding debts than Martin Property Group, which previously submitted a bid that Gordon Brothers rejected.

But doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer, as there is little evidence they meet Gordon Brothers' tests, including whether they have the money and whether they would be good long-term owners of Poundland.

Sources pointed to the appointment of Andrew Brode to Xyra's board as a sign of its credibility. Brode works for RWS - a company that provides AI solutions for businesses.

Judith MacKenzie, head of Downing Fund Managers, told the BBC Brode is "well known and very credible" among small businesses in the UK.

But she said there is "hardly any information" publicly available about Xyra. "So, although some of the people look good, I can't find any evidence to say that they've got the money to back it up yet," MacKenzie added.

Gordon Brothers said: "Our intent throughout the comprehensive sale process has been to protect as many jobs as possible and preserve value in order to deliver the best available outcome for all the people, creditors and local communities who care about this business as much as we do."

Both Reynolds and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have questioned why a deal for the future of Poundland has not yet been made.

Though Xyra made an offer to take over the whole business, it is unclear whether it would keep Poundland together as its owner or break the company up.

Several Poundland suppliers have said they would also go bust if the retailer collapses. Its founder Steve Smith said two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, those who solely work for Poundland, would be caught up in the collapse.

He added that not only would Poundland's 12,000 staff be affected in that case, but potentially up to 30,000 overall.

articles.title: Garth Brooks: Country legend returns to Belfast with 2027 gigs
articles.summary: Brooks will play two outdoor concerts at Boucher Road Playing Fields on 21 and 22 May 2027.
articles.body:
American country music legend Garth Brooks will return to perform in Northern Ireland for the first time since 1998 with two gigs in Belfast in May of next year.

Brooks will play two outdoor concerts at Boucher Road Playing Fields on 21 and 22 May 2027.

His last gigs in Northern Ireland were a five-night run at the King's Hall in Belfast in November 1998, after which he said the reaction from fans left his ears "ringing for three days".

Next year's concerts in Belfast will be the first of 10 on the island of Ireland, with two shows each in Galway, Kilkenny, Limerick and Cork.

In a post on X , Brooks said: "I've been dreaming of this a long time, Ireland... love, g."

Some of the Oklahoma singer's biggest hits include Friends in Low Places, If Tomorrow Never Comes and Callin' Baton Rouge.

Brooks is the biggest selling artist in US history as the only artist to pass 200 million albums sold.

In a promo for next year's shows, Brooks said: "This has been a dream of mine since the first time we played Ireland. Once you get a taste of how the Irish love music, you can't play there enough."

Brooks last performed in Ireland in September 2022.

More than 400,000 tickets were sold for five concerts at Dublin's Croke Park.

In 2014, Brooks cancelled a five-night run at Croke Park after Dublin City Council granted licences for just three of the five.

During the controversy, Brooks said: "I have faith that Dublin City Council will make the best decision for the people of Ireland.

"For us, it is five shows or none at all. To choose which shows to do and which shows not to do, would be like asking to choose one child over another."

Dublin City Council said at the time, that it would "not be appropriate to grant five consecutive nights of concerts".

They said the scale of the concerts was "unprecedented" and would lead to "an unacceptable level of disruption" for residents and businesses near Croke Park.

Residents near the GAA stadium had threatened legal action after the initial two concerts were increased to five.

After Brooks pulled out of the concerts, it led to the Irish government announcing new licensing laws.

It meant concert promoters in the Republic of Ireland would not be allowed to sell tickets before consulting with local authorities.

The five Dublin concerts in 2022 were also described as "unacceptable" by a residents group representing people who live near Croke Park.

articles.title: Titanic's owners received $5 million within 30 days of the sinking; 114 years later, original insurance document resurfaces and could fetch $67,000 at auction
articles.summary: More than a century after the Titanic sank in the North Atlantic, an unusual piece of paperwork connected to the doomed liner's final voyage has
articles.body: More than a century after the Titanic sank in the North Atlantic, an unusual piece of paperwork connected to the doomed liner's final voyage has resurfaced. An original insurance document linked to the ship's $5 million total-loss cover, arranged just weeks before the disaster, is set to go under the hammer in Britain, with an estimated price of up to $67,000. The document is being offered by British auction house Henry Aldridge and Son at its November 21 auction in Devizes, England. It carries an estimate of £30,000 to £50,000, equivalent to approximately $40,000 to $67,000.The document is particularly striking because it records insurance protection for a ship that was widely believed to be virtually unsinkable, yet disappeared beneath the Atlantic less than a month after the policy took effect. Its most remarkable detail, however, is what happened after the disaster: Titanic's owners received the full insurance payout within 30 days of the sinking, even as families of those who died faced a much longer wait for compensation.Just weeks before the Titanic disasterThe insurance arrangement was taken out by the Oceanic Steam Navigation Company, the parent company of the White Star Line, which operated Titanic. According to the auction description and reports by PEOPLE, the ship was covered for a total loss of $5 million through an arrangement involving 77 insurers. One of the major participants was Atlantic Mutual Insurance Company, which covered $100,000 of the risk. The resurfaced document comes from Atlantic Mutual's archives and records its individual share of the wider insurance arrangement. It should not be confused with a single policy showing that Atlantic Mutual alone insured the entire ship for $5 million.The document was signed on March 27, 1912, with coverage taking effect on March 30 at 7 pm and continuing until March 30, 1913. It also contains a handwritten addition extending protection to Titanic's journey from Belfast to Southampton and the risk associated with its sea trials. The timing makes the document particularly significant. Titanic departed Southampton on April 10, 1912, on its maiden voyage to New York. Four days later, on the night of April 14, it struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic. The ship sank in the early hours of April 15, killing approximately 1,500 people.The insurance settlement was completed far more quickly than many might expect following a disaster of such scale. Lloyd's, which had arranged more than £1 million in hull insurance for Titanic, confirms in its historical records that insurers paid the claims in full within 30 days. Lloyd's records show that the ship's hull alone was insured for £1 million. The risk was distributed among several companies and more than 50 Lloyd's syndicates, with individual participants taking different portions of the cover. The premium for the hull insurance was £7,500.The $5 million total-loss cover reported in connection with the resurfaced Atlantic Mutual document was part of the wider insurance arrangement. The auction house says the limits of Atlantic Mutual's policy were also paid within 30 days of the sinking.Families waited years for compensationAuctioneer Andrew Aldridge told PEOPLE that it was extraordinary that the owners received their payout within a month of the disaster, when the funerals of many victims had barely taken place. He also described the words "total loss" in the document as particularly striking given how soon after the policy was issued the ship was destroyed.According to Aldridge, families who pursued negligence claims had to wait four years for compensation, eventually receiving a combined total of $663,000. His comparison highlights the difference between the insurance arrangements protecting the vessel's owners and the lengthy process faced by people seeking compensation for the human losses.Titanic carried 2,224 passengers and crew. It had only 20 lifeboats, with capacity for 1,178 people. Lloyd's historical account records that 1,514 people perished, making the sinking one of the deadliest peacetime maritime disasters.The ship's loss also became a major event in the history of marine insurance. Lloyd's records describe how news of the sinking initially arrived through wireless telegraphy, with conflicting reports circulating for days. Some newspapers even believed the ship had survived and was being towed to Halifax.How the 114-year-old document resurfacedThe insurance document remained among the historical records of Atlantic Mutual, a US insurer founded in 1838. The company was eventually placed into liquidation in 2011 after suffering financial difficulties, including losses connected to claims arising from the September 11, 2001 attacks.Following its liquidation, historical material from its archives was included in an exhibition in New York. A dealer subsequently purchased the Titanic insurance document, according to the auction house and PEOPLE.Aldridge said the auction house had been unable to locate another surviving original insurance document relating to Titanic and described the item as unique to its knowledge. The estimate of up to £50,000 reflects its rarity and its connection to one of the most famous maritime disasters in history.The insurance document will not be the only Titanic-related artefact offered at the November 21 sale. Original shipbuilding plans used by Harland and Wolff, the Belfast company that constructed the liner, are also due to be auctioned.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: She secretly began lifting weights despite her parents' objections; Kerala bodybuilder Bhumika Senthilkumar went on to win national titles and international gold, changing her family's view of women's bodybuilding
articles.summary: For Bhumika Senthilkumar, bodybuilding began as a dream she had to pursue without her family's approval.
articles.body: For Bhumika Senthilkumar, bodybuilding began as a dream she had to pursue without her family's approval. Growing up in Palakkad, Kerala, she wanted to take part in sports but says she was an overprotected child who was rarely allowed to join physical activities at school. Even running during physical training periods was not something she could freely do.As a teenager, she began exploring fitness on her own, watching workout videos and following professional women bodybuilders on social media. What started as curiosity gradually became a serious ambition. Her family was not convinced that bodybuilding was the right path for her, but Bhumika continued to look for a way into the sport.In November 2025, that determination took her to the international stage. She won gold in the Women's Wellness category and bronze in Sports Physique at the 16th World Bodybuilding and Physique Sports Championship in Batam City, Indonesia. The medals marked a major moment in her career and helped change how her family viewed her chosen profession.A dream that began with watching other women liftBhumika's interest in bodybuilding grew as she watched women athletes train and compete. She wanted to build her own strength and eventually participate in professional competitions. Finding the right mentor, however, took time. In July 2022, she contacted coach Abhil John Manuel of Fitness Factory in Kochi's Kadavanthra through Instagram. Her first message did not receive a response. She later visited his gym with her friend Glen Martin, who also wanted to pursue professional bodybuilding.Manuel asked them to join the gym and train for three months. That meeting became the beginning of a more structured journey for Bhumika. She began working towards competitive bodybuilding while also pursuing fashion design studies. The decision meant managing two demanding commitments. She often travelled between college and the gym, sometimes sleeping for only a few hours. There were days when training felt difficult, but she continued to follow her routine, adjusting the intensity when she could not give her full effort.The work behind the medalsPreparing for an international bodybuilding competition required considerable discipline. In the months leading up to the 2025 championship, Bhumika's training became more intensive. She initially worked out twice a day, eventually increasing the schedule to multiple sessions along with posing practice. Her diet also changed as competition approached. She restricted sugar and followed a carefully planned food routine that included chicken, eggs and vegetables, along with supplements. Managing the cost of training and preparation was another challenge.A few weeks before the championship, she sprained her leg, raising doubts about whether she would be able to compete. However, she continued working towards the event with support from her coach and gym community. At Batam, Indonesia, her efforts resulted in two medals. She won gold in Women's Wellness on November 16, 2025, and had secured bronze in Sports Physique a day earlier. The result was especially meaningful because she was representing India at a global competition.Three years to change her family's mindWinning medals was not the only milestone Bhumika had been hoping for. She also wanted her parents to understand why bodybuilding mattered to her. According to her account in an interview with *The Week*, her family took around three years to accept her decision. Her mother had initially encouraged her to spend time with friends rather than devote so much time to workouts. The family's concerns reflected the hesitation many women face when choosing a sport that challenges conventional ideas about femininity.After her international success, the response at home began to change. Her parents and others welcomed her at the airport when she returned from Indonesia. Bhumika also shared that her family now helps prepare her diet meals. She has spoken about the comments women bodybuilders often receive about their physiques. Some people assume that lifting weights will make women look less feminine. Bhumika, however, sees strength training as a way to build fitness and confidence.Beyond the competition stageBodybuilding has brought Bhumika recognition, but she has also spoken about the pressures that come with competing. As a wellness athlete, she has to prepare her physique for judging, and the changes in her body during the off-season can take some adjustment. Competing also means putting one's appearance before an audience and dealing with public opinions. Her coach, Abhil John Manuel, has described her as a driven athlete who remains focused on improving, even after winning medals. Bhumika, meanwhile, wants to continue competing and defending her title.Her journey is not simply about lifting weights or winning trophies. It is about pursuing a sporting ambition when the people closest to her initially struggled to understand it. From following fitness videos as a teenager to winning gold on an international stage, Bhumika has built a career through consistency, support from her coach and a willingness to keep going. Perhaps one of the most personal victories came after the medals, when her family began standing beside her dream rather than questioning it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Canadian woman Seema David began feeding people in need from shared kitchens in Toronto in 2013; she later built 5N2 into a food charity with its own indoor farms
articles.summary: A Canadian woman who began preparing meals in shared community and church kitchens in 2013 has built a community food initiative into an organisation that
articles.body: A Canadian woman who began preparing meals in shared community and church kitchens in 2013 has built a community food initiative into an organisation that supports people in need through meal distribution, food rescue and urban farming. Seema David started the project with limited financial resources and help from volunteers after noticing homeless people during her daily journeys through Toronto. She initially prepared meals three days a week and used shared community and church kitchens to reach local communities.According to her company profile, 5N2, the first meals were prepared and distributed in spring 2013. The initiative gradually expanded through food donations, community partnerships, and volunteer support. The initiative moved into its own rented kitchen in 2018 and, in 2022, into a custom-designed facility that houses indoor farming.How did Seema David’s early life in Canada inspire her food charityBefore 5N2 took shape, Seema had spent several years adjusting to life in Canada after moving there from Dubai in 2007 with her three children. The early years brought financial difficulties, uncertainty over her husband's employment and challenges as her children settled into new schools. She later worked as an assistant to a dean at George Brown College for two and a half years, but her contract was not renewed when another employee secured the permanent position.During this period, her daily encounters with people living in poverty made her think about ways to support the community. She wanted to use whatever resources she had to provide food to people who could not afford a meal. This idea eventually became the starting point of her charitable work.From a church kitchen to a food charity in CanadaDuring her early years in Canada, Seema often walked to and from work to save money on transport. Along the way, she regularly saw homeless people near Union Station and downtown Toronto. Despite her own financial struggles, seeing people without food made Seema consider how she could help by providing them with hot meals.Her church had moved into a building with a large kitchen that was rarely used. She asked its leadership for permission to use the space, but the decision was delayed for six months because of concerns about allowing homeless people into the building. Seema continued exploring other options and discussed the idea with former colleagues, church members and community contacts in the local area.The community support behind Seema David’s first mealsA community service centre in Scarborough eventually allowed Seema to use its semi-commercial kitchen one day a week. Another church offered access to a smaller kitchen, while her own church later provided a time slot for a seniors group. With no formal funding, Seema used the family savings that remained to buy basic supplies and equipment.An unemployed chef volunteered to help with equipment purchases, menu planning, and food preparation. Their collaboration lasted five years. In spring 2013, the first meals were prepared and distributed to the local community. The kitchen initially operated three days a week, and Seema continued despite limited resources and concerns from family members about the money and time she was giving to the project.The shift from family funding to regular food donationsBy the end of 2015, the kitchen was preparing and distributing food from Monday to Friday. Meals were cooked in the church kitchen and delivered to several locations across East Scarborough. For three years, most expenses had been covered by Seema’s family and local church members. In December 2015, her family told her their funds had been exhausted.The first formal donation came from the University of Toronto’s gospel choir, which gave the kitchen about $2,000 from its charity concerts. In 2016, Second Harvest began regular weekly deliveries of rescued food after assessing the kitchen’s storage, food handling and distribution arrangements. Mama Earth Organics also began supplying fresh organic produce each week.How did 5N2 expand its operations with a new facilityFrom 2013 to December 2018, the soup kitchen operated mainly from the church kitchen in East Toronto. As demand and volunteer numbers increased, Seema sought a dedicated space. In 2018, she found an unused commercial kitchen in a facility behind the church and agreed to rent it for $2,000 a month. The team cleaned and restored the premises before moving equipment from the church.In November 2022, 5N2 moved into a custom-designed facility that housed its two vertical farming units. By the end of 2023, the first indoor crops, including lettuce, herbs, and fresh greens, had been harvested. The growing team used some produce in meals, while the rest was sold to local restaurants in the area.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Losing gambler energy': Iran speaker mocks Vance's midterm assessment
articles.summary: Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has openly mocked US vice president over his post on X following a less than ideal midterm election
articles.body: Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has openly mocked US vice president over his post on X following a less than ideal midterm election defeat, comparing him to a gambler unable to walk away from a losing bet.In a post on X responding to Vance's lengthy assessment of the election results, Ghalibaf wrote: “Losing gambler energy, can't walk away from the table.” He accused the US administration of preparing for the next phase of the war while America was “teetering on an Israel-First cliff”.“Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?” he added.Ghalibaf was responding to Vance's post in which the vice president acknowledged that the Iran war had contributed to Republican losses, arguing that many voters who supported president Donald Trump and Vance in 2024 had switched to Democratic candidates in the midterms.Vance said the main problem was not voter turnout, as Republican supporters had largely turned out to vote, but that a significant section of the party's previous supporters had voted against it.Citing feedback from a pollster who had accurately anticipated the scale of the Republican defeat, Vance identified four major reasons behind the voter shift: opposition to the war, concerns over the cost of living and inflation, dissatisfaction with the administration's “America First” approach and calls for a change in Washington's relationship with Israel.“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote, adding that any honest assessment of the Republican defeat must begin with the conflict.He also criticised those who had opposed calls for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, saying their political advice had proved misguided. Vance argued that the administration would face attempts to shift blame for the election results, but said the war remained the central issue behind the party's losses.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kanya King to be honoured with stone laid at Queen's Park school
articles.summary: King tirelessly championed music of black origin, and funded the first awards out of her own pocket.
articles.body:
A commemorative stone is to be laid in London in honour of the late Mobo founder Kanya King, to mark the 30th anniversary of the music ceremony.

The Mobo awards music ceremony - which celebrates black music, culture and excellence from the UK and abroad - was launched by King in 1996.

Through Mobo, King is credited with playing a major role in bringing black music and culture to the mainstream in the UK. King died this summer from colon cancer at the age of 57.

The Paving the Way stone will be unveiled on 18 November at her former school, Queens Park Community College in Queen's Park, north-west London.

King was awarded a CBE in 2018 for her contributions to music and culture.

A BBC programme to mark the 30th anniversary, presented by DJ Target, will take viewers through some of the most defining moments, performances, and cultural milestones from the Mobo stage since it was first founded.

The programme, MOBO 30: Iconic Moments , will air on 11 November on BBC One and iPlayer.

The anniversary celebrations will also see V&A East Storehouse present a special temporary display featuring a selection of memorabilia from the Mobo archive.

articles.title: Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go?
articles.summary: The BBC's economics editor views one more interest rate as likely, but thinks that will be all.
articles.body:
Interest rates have risen to 4% and the Bank of England has indicated there are more rises to come. The question is how many? There is a split on the rate-setting committee here.

Three of the nine voting members referred to "rises" plural. One member voted for a bigger increase, to 4.25%. Three referred to just one more including governor Andrew Bailey.

My read on this is that the expectation is for one more rise in February. Two and done, but it depends.

It is painful for those on variable mortgages, but should not be seen as the start of a cycle of hikes.

Predicting where interest rates will go is like throwing darts at a board that constantly moves around the wall, with expectations of how long the Iran War will last and its impact on the economy and prices lurching from day to day.

The Bank's forecasts indicate inflation is heading to just under 5% next spring as a typical household energy bill surges by 27% in January to £2,150 a year.

Why have they raised now? High and rising inflation risks a further cycle of self fulfilling expectations of rising prices. It hasn't been seen so far, however. The war has lasted for 9 months, and led to oil prices used in the forecast averaging $108 a barrel.

And yet on the day they have announced the rate rise, the oil price is actually 13% lower than that having fallen in the run up and after the US mid term elections, reflecting expectations or guesses that President Trump will now retreat or deescalate from the Iran war.

The other notable factor is that the UK economy is performing much better than forecasts and expectations. This is underlined by the Bank of England's latest forecasts.

Growth has been 0.6%, and 0.5% in the first two quarters of the year. It is heading for 0.7%, the Bank said, between July and September, before slowing in the three months to the end of the year. Unemployment has stabilised, actually falling a little.

Some of this has fed through into a better performing currency , with sterling at its highest level since the Brexit referendum, when measured against a basket of currencies. This can help rein in inflation by making imports cheaper.

So, this is an unusual type of uncertainty. Even the expected further rise, probably in February next year is conditional on the war continuing.

The Bank of England stopped waiting for President Trump's war to end today, but perhaps the Democrats' resounding victory in the US midterm elections will stop the inflationary wave? The Bank has thrown a tentative first dart, and there is probably another to come.

articles.title: Delhi riots case: Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam challenge Delhi HC's bail refusal in Supreme Court
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Jailed activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam have separately moved the Supreme Court challenging the Delhi high court's September 30 order
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Jailed activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam have separately moved the Supreme Court challenging the Delhi high court's September 30 order refusing them bail in the 2020 Delhi riots larger conspiracy case.In their pleas, both activists argue that they should be granted bail as the prosecution has failed to examine a single witness despite them having spent more than six years in custody as an undertrial. They also pointed out that the one-year period stipulated by the Supreme Court for filing fresh bail pleas was nearing its end.The petition by Imam stated that the chargesheet in the case was filed on September 25, 2020, naming 18 accused and citing more than 900 witnesses, including 47 protected witnesses. However, the prosecution is yet to examine even one witness, Imam submitted.Khalid in his plea pointed out that the prosecution has failed to examine protected witnesses and the one-year embargo imposed by the top court is about to expire and therefore prolonged incarceration would violate Article 21 of the Constitution.Article 21 of the Constitution asserts that no person shall be deprived of their life except according to the procedure established by law. This means that every individual has the right to live, and their life cannot be taken away except in accordance with the prescribed legal procedures.The Delhi high court on September 30 rejected the fresh bail pleas of Khalid and Imam, holding that it was bound by judicial discipline and could not modify the Supreme Court's January 5 order. The top court had allowed the two to approach the courts again after the examination of protected witnesses or after the expiry of one year, whichever came earlier.The two activists had approached the high court after a trial court rejected their bail applications for the third time on July 4. The trial court had said it had "no option but to follow" the Supreme Court's January 5 order and could neither entertain their pleas nor grant relief.During the high court proceedings, senior advocate Trideep Pais, appearing for Khalid, had argued that there were three "small changes in circumstances" since the earlier proceedings. He pointed out that charges had not yet been framed and prosecution witnesses had not been examined. Pais also relied on a Supreme Court judgment to support his submissions.Opposing the pleas, Delhi police maintained that Khalid and Imam were the "masterminds" of the riots and could not seek bail on parity with other accused. The police argued that the Supreme Court had previously categorised them as part of the alleged conspiracy's "command authority" and held that their risk profiles justified continued detention.On January 5, the Supreme Court upheld the Delhi high court's September 2, 2025 decision denying bail to Khalid and Imam, while granting relief to five co-accused — Gulfisha Fatima, Meeran Haider, Shifa Ur Rehman, Mohammad Saleem Khan and Shadab Ahmad.A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and N V Anjaria had observed that there was a prima facie case against Khalid and Imam under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA). It also noted that their alleged roles were distinct from those of the other accused, describing them as the "ideological drivers" of the alleged conspiracy.Khalid and Imam have been in custody since September 2020 and August 2020, respectively. They are accused of being among the masterminds of the larger conspiracy behind the February 2020 riots in northeast Delhi, which left 53 people dead and more than 700 injured.The violence erupted amid protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act (CAA) and the proposed National Register of Citizens (NRC).The Supreme Court has previously also referred to a larger bench the question of prolonged incarceration of undertrials booked under the UAPA in view of the law's stringent bail conditions.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Vermont aviation CEO won approval for a 900-foot runway on his 130-acre estate, but a neighbour says she has spent $300,000 fighting the plan as appeals continue over the private airstrip
articles.summary: Community spirit has turned to a lengthy court fight at a private airstrip in a quiet Vermont mountain town where neighbors used to welcome new residents
articles.body: Community spirit has turned to a lengthy court fight at a private airstrip in a quiet Vermont mountain town where neighbors used to welcome new residents with homemade casseroles and offers of riding lessons. A wealthy aviation entrepreneur who wants to fly direct from his estate and a neighbour who is determined to stop the runway changing the character of the surrounding countryside are at the heart of the issue. The project has been approved by several authorities but is still the subject of appeals, with both sides defending their cases.Private airstrip divides mountain communityThe Boston Globe reported that the feud is between Beta Technologies electric aircraft maker chief executive Kyle Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who bought a 130-acre property in Lincoln, Vermont, in 2021. Clark wanted to construct a 900-foot grass runway on their estate so he could fly small, gas-powered planes right from home.The proposal immediately raised hackles among nearby residents, notably Marilyn Ganahl, who owns a 105-acre horse farm and nature preserve next door. Ganahl has estimated she has spent about $300,000, mostly funding the fight against the airstrip.Since then the dispute has broadened to encompass whether a person can use private land for aviation purposes. Residents have expressed concerns about the safety and noise of aircraft, the landscape and the risk of disruption to a community known for its rural character.The controversy also has divided residents, some who value the jobs and economic benefits Clark’s company has provided to Vermont, but who also are uneasy about the increasing neighborhood strife, The Boston Globe reported.How the project got regulatory approvalClark has long been interested in flying. He’s long wanted to fly an aircraft from his own property, having taken time away from Harvard to play professional hockey while pursuing pilot training.According to News From The States, he bought the Lincoln property and in 2022 approached the town seeking permission to build the runway. Ganahl appealed the zoning administrator’s initial approval of the application. Then the town’s zoning board rejected the proposal, and Lincoln’s Development Review Board voted it down, too, in 2023.Clark appealed the local rulings in Vermont’s Environmental Court, News From The States said. Later rulings allowed the land-use part of his application to go forward, sending aviation safety and related issues to federal and state agencies.In June 2025, the Federal Aviation Administration made a conditional determination that the airstrip could operate under certain restrictions. These included private use during the day and conditions to avoid conflict with neighbouring flight paths, municipal structures and existing visual flight rules.The FAA denied an appeal by opponents on July 28, 2026. The Vermont Transportation Board later approved the project Oct. 8, moving Clark a step closer to getting the go-ahead to operate the runway.Neighbours continue with legal challengeThe regulatory approvals have not muted the opposition. Ganahl and fellow resident Sarah Laird filed an appeal with the Vermont Supreme Court asking for a review of the Transportation Board’s October decision, News From The States reports. The board has also been asked to hold a certificate of operation until the court makes a ruling.They are worried about the absence of a public hearing during the Transportation Board’s review. Instead, the board reviewed written correspondence from residents in its deliberations. Opponents say this prevented several interested parties from adequately presenting their concerns.Safety is another major stumbling block. Neighbours have raised questions about whether a short runway in difficult terrain can provide safe take-offs and landings.Their concerns were backed up by an assessment prepared by aviation consultant Lee Moak, who looked at the area’s topography and the proposed runway. News From The States reported Moak found the airstrip may not fit in with its surroundings and recommended nine more steps before approval. They also argue that the FAA did not properly consider his assessment in rejecting their appeal.So they have appealed to a federal appeals court to try to overturn the FAA decision and the battle continues, at both the state and federal levels.A wealthy business man and a pricey stand offThe financial resources available to both sides has also become another defining characteristic of the controversy. Clark is the head of Beta Technologies, a rapidly expanding electric aviation company with some 1,500 employees that has become one of Vermont’s signature businesses.Clark has admitted to spending an extraordinary amount on legal proceedings and other costs related to the runway, the Boston Globe reported. Meanwhile, he purchased a separate property in Charlotte, Vermont, for $14 million that already has an authorized airstrip. He now uses the property when flying to Beta’s head office in Burlington.The Clarks have also invested in the local community, purchasing the historic Lincoln General Store with a business partner in 2024. The group paid $457,000 for the establishment and has invested additional money in renovations.But those contributions haven't necessarily improved relations with opponents, some of whom remain uneasy about the family's influence in town.Permission to build is not permission to flyThe runway has not been activated, notwithstanding approvals. Clark must fulfill the requirements of the FAA and the Vermont Agency of Transportation before the Transportation Board can issue the final Certificate of Operation, News From The States reported.The continuing appeals mean the project could face further delays even after years of regulatory proceedings.The argument has become more than an aviation facility for Lincoln. It has considered the relationship between private property rights, public safety and the responsibilities of being part of a close-knit community.Ganahl and other residents say they are determined to fight the decisions, while Clark says he has followed all the proper legal procedures. The 900-foot runway on the Vermont estate remains the centre of an increasingly costly neighbourhood battle until the outstanding appeals are resolved.Image Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: Two more arrests following Chandler's Ford Halloween party stabbing
articles.summary: Two 16-year-old boys from Southampton are arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.
articles.body:
Two more arrests have been made by police investigating the stabbing of five teenagers at a Halloween party in Hampshire.

Police were called shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday to a home in Park Road in Chandler's Ford where an "unknown group" had gained entry to the event over a garden fence.

One boy, 17, remains in hospital in a serious condition. The other four boys, who were all injured, have since been discharged.

On Thursday, police said two 16-year-old boys from Southampton had been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. This brings the total number of arrests to six.

Two 16-year-old boys from Southampton arrested earlier in the week remain in custody after the court granted officer more time to continue questioning them.

Two more boys, who were also arrested and questioned as part of the investigation, have been released on bail.

The officer leading the investigation, Det Ch Insp Elizabeth Pirie, said: "During an investigation like this one, information is provided to us which will require us to make an arrest in order to secure possible evidence and take someone's account.

"We have been working closely with the CPS to assess the available evidence and review whether there is sufficient grounds for charges to be authorised or if there is additional enquiries which need to be made.

"Today, we have released two of the boys we have arrested on police bail while we continue with our investigation. This bail comes with strict conditions in place, and this is monitored to ensure those conditions are being complied with."

Pirie said the force had a large number of officers working on the case as it tried to piece together the movements of those it believed were involved.

Hampshire Police is continuing to appeal for witnesses, and anyone who may have information, to come forward and has thanked those it has already spoken to.

Pirie added: "I know that for those who were at the party on Saturday, this has been a really distressing time, but their help has been so important."

articles.title: Putin not invited to G20 summit in Manchester, says Andy Burnham
articles.summary: The prime minister has said sanctions against Russia mean Putin will not attend the summit in November 2027.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Vladimir Putin is not invited to the G20 summit in Manchester.

Asked whether the Russian president would be invited to the annual meeting, which the UK is hosting in November 2027, Burnham said "no" because of sanctions against the Kremlin.

The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

But US president Donald Trump has sparked controversy by inviting Putin to this year's G20, which he will host in Miami in December. The Kremlin has not yet said whether Putin will attend.

Russia is a member of the G20 - a group of 19 nations, the European Union and African Union - while Ukraine is not, but the ongoing war in Ukraine has loomed large over recent summits.

Putin has not attended any major global summit since he launched his invasion and ongoing war in Ukraine.

Asked about inviting him to the G20 in Manchester in 2027, Burnham told The Economist he "will not be coming because of an outstanding sanction" on senior Russian figures.

He said the meeting would provide "a real opportunity" to work with Chinese president Xi Jinping on safety regulations for artificial intelligence (AI).

Pressed on whether the UK could bring the US and China around the same table to agree on global AI supervision, Burnham said: "As I sit here today, that feels challenging, but we've got to hold out the need to find global agreements on AI.

"If we don't, the risks of recent times will magnify, they will significantly intensify.

"So you've got to go into it with that aim."

His decision not to include Putin in next year's gathering in Manchester comes after European diplomats refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in October.

The so-called "family photo" would usually include representatives from all nations in attendance, but this year it was cancelled.

The US decision to invite Lavrov in the first place - which itself came after further public rows between Trump and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky - also attracted criticism.

Discussing Ukraine, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told Lavrov at the summit: "Let me say this directly to the Russian foreign minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is."

The UK last hosted the G20 summit in 2009. Next year's two-day event will take place in the Manchester Central Convention Centre in Manchester city centre and host thousands of diplomats and delegates, as well as world leaders.

The government has said it will use its G20 presidency in 2027 to "reinforce global economic stability" and "benefit people in every part of the UK".

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India is reportedly nearing a fresh defence deal with the Philippines for the supply of nearly 60 BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles in a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India is reportedly nearing a fresh defence deal with the Philippines for the supply of nearly 60 BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles in a potential agreement worth $700 million to $800 million.The information comes from a Reuters report citing three sources with direct knowledge of the development.Manila is expected to procure around five BrahMos systems as New Delhi moves towards completing deliveries under an earlier $375 million agreement signed in 2022.Two Indian sources told Reuters that the proposed order would include nearly 60 missiles."Manila has shown interest again to procure about 5 systems of the BrahMos and they now view India as a very reliable partner," one of the Indian sources said.Philippine defence ministry spokesperson Arsenio Andolong told Reuters that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr had expressed interest in acquiring additional BrahMos missiles, but did not provide further details.Philippine defence secretary Gilberto Teodoro also indicated the country's interest in expanding the procurement. Speaking virtually at the Delhi Defence Dialogue on Wednesday, he said Manila hoped to acquire more BrahMos units and had submitted a wish list to Indian authorities to adapt the system more closely to the country's requirements.Also read: 1,500-km BrahMos expected in 2-3 yrs, lighter missile version prototype by 2027-28: CEOManila seeks to strengthen coastal defencesThe proposed purchase comes as the Philippines steps up efforts to modernise its military and strengthen its coastal defences amid escalating tensions with China over competing territorial claims in the South China Sea. The two countries have been involved in several confrontations in the disputed waters in recent years.The BrahMos missile, jointly developed by India and Russia, is among the world's fastest cruise missiles and can be launched from land, naval vessels and aircraft. Interest in the weapon system has grown since the four-day conflict between India and Pakistan last year, during which India used BrahMos missiles in combat for the first time.India has also been expanding its overseas sales of the system. In July, New Delhi announced the supply of BrahMos missiles to Indonesia and signed an agreement with Vietnam. It is also holding discussions with several other countries, including the United Arab Emirates, Thailand, South Africa and Brazil.India's defence exports reached 384.24 billion rupees ($4.11 billion) in the financial year ending March, marking an increase of more than 62 per cent from the previous year, according to government data.

articles.title: 'Flawed' Army training contributed to Max George's death, coroner rules
articles.summary: A coroner rules Second Lt Max George's death on Salisbury Plain was an accident.
articles.body:
An Army officer's accidental death during a training exercise was contributed to by "flawed" training and a faulty alarm system, a coroner has concluded.

Second Lt Max George, 26, died on Salisbury Plain after struggling with a piece of "snagged" kit as he left a Warrior armoured vehicle, which then reversed into him, an inquest into his death heard.

Victoria Neale, who represented George's family, said the inquest provided his loved ones with "important answers" and provided a "degree of accountability".

The Ministry of Defence (MOD) vowed to respond to points raised during the inquest and said it had already made several safety improvements.

The inquest heard that George, from Durham, was stood by the open rear door of the Warrior on 21 June 2022 when the exercise commander gave the order to reverse the armoured vehicle.

The 26-year-old died at the scene near Everleigh from multiple traumatic injuries, Wiltshire and Swindon Coroner's Court was told.

Recording a narrative conclusion, Coroner Ian Singleton said the training of the student commander who gave the command had been flawed.

Brigadier Giles Malec, head of the Army Safety Group, said the service recognised "the seriousness of the failures which led to Max's tragic death" and would "look to rectify any additional failures identified". He apologised to the family on the second day of the inquest.

Warrior vehicles are no longer allowed to reverse with the rear door open and visual checks are required before any movement.

Reward offered to help solve dog walker's murder

Altar Stone mystery continues as theory overturned

Market and town halls: Historic sites being left to ruin

The inquest was told an alarm on the Warrior had been faulty since 2018.

Lt Col Graham Watson, who led a service inquiry into the incident, had told the inquest that if the alarm was not faulty: "The built in alarm would have alarmed because the rear doors were open, and had that gone off the driver would have almost certainly stopped."

He said George's exit from the Warrior would have created a "clunking noise", which may have led the commander to assume he was safely off the vehicle and had shut the doors.

Singleton said the alarm on the Warrior had not been repaired despite it being reported.

The coroner said there had been no effective regime for maintaining the vehicle which struck George and it was not routinely used for disembarking troops.

The MOD said it was set to replace its entire Warrior fleet from 2027.

Singleton said he would decide whether to issue a prevention of future deaths note at a later date.

"Whilst nothing can undo the family's loss, it is hoped that these measures, if implemented and adhered to, will reduce the risk of a similar tragedy occurring in the future," Neale, from Pepperells Solicitors, said.

Wiltshire and Swindon Coroner's Court was told George was a well-respected officer and earned the Queen's Medal for best cadet when he passed out from the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst.

His commanding officer, Lt Col Jim Hadfield OBE, described the recruit as "a star that burned bright" with "selfless compassion."

George had been head boy at Durham School, studied Russian at Newcastle University and obtained a Distinction in his Masters in Eastern European and Eurasian Studies with Russian at Glasgow University, the court was told.

As part of the 5 Rifles, he had been taking part in Exercise Combat Spirit on the day of the incident.
